subject: Civil Engineering
title: Reservoir Sedimentation
description: A short lesson to help you apply Reservoir Sedimentation.

hook.text: Every river carries sediment. When a dam stops the flow, sediment fills the reservoir.

buildup.text: Silt, sand, and clay settle behind the dam — slowly reducing water storage capacity year by year.

discovery.text: Some reservoirs lose 1-2% of capacity annually — within decades, they become useless.

twist.text: Flushing — opening low-level outlets during floods — can scour sediment out downstream.

climax.text: China's Sanmenxia Dam lost 90% of capacity to silt in just four years after completion.

punchline.text: Dams stop water — but they also stop sediment. That slow filling is their expiration date.

quiz.question: What happened to China's Sanmenxia Dam's capacity shortly after construction?
options: Earthquakes cracked the dam and reduced its structural capacity
Sediment filled 90% of the reservoir within four years
Drought reduced the river flow to unusable levels

details.summary: Reservoir sedimentation occurs as rivers deposit their suspended and bed-load sediment when flow velocity decreases upon entering a reservoir. Over decades, sediment accumulates and reduces storage capacity.
details.whyItMatters: Sedimentation is slowly destroying the storage capacity of reservoirs worldwide. Unlike most infrastructure problems, it is essentially irreversible, making currently stored sediment a permanent loss of capacity.
takeaways: Rivers decelerate upon entering reservoirs, dropping their sediment load
Global reservoirs lose approximately 1% of total capacity per year to sediment
Sediment management strategies include flushing, dredging, and bypass tunnels

faq.question: Can sediment be removed from reservoirs once it has accumulated?
faq.answer: Mechanical dredging removes sediment but is extremely expensive for large volumes. Sediment flushing lowers the reservoir and uses high-velocity flow to scour deposits through low-level outlets. Sediment bypass tunnels divert sediment-laden flood flows around the reservoir.

faq.question: What happens to a river downstream when a dam traps its sediment?
faq.answer: Without its natural sediment supply, downstream water erodes the riverbed and banks, called clear-water erosion. Riverbeds scour deeper, groundwater tables drop, bridge foundations become exposed, and deltas shrink.
